claimed.question: Can N friendly Builder Bots out-heal M enemy Builder Bots grinding a forward turret, and is a forward turret therefore holdable? (Task 1.1, fcode 2.3.6)
claimed.headline: Healing beats grinding exactly 4:1 in titanium and 2:1 in HP — one healer cancels two grinders for 1 Ti/round against their 4 Ti/round — so a forward turret escorted by 2 parked Builder Bots is mathematically unkillable by grinding, because a 1x1 turret has only 4 orthogonal contact tiles and 2 healers (+8 HP/round) always out-pace the at-most-2 grinders (-4 HP/round) that can still reach it.

claimed.design_impact:
FORWARD TURRETS ARE HOLDABLE. The premise that a 40 Ti Builder Bot destroys a 310 Ti forward Sentinel is true only for an UNESCORTED turret, and the answer costs 20 Ti of healing, not a design change.

The rule to build into the bot: net HP/round on a forward turret = 6k - 8, where k is the number of the turret's 4 orthogonal tiles we occupy. k>=2 is positive, k=1 is -2, k=0 is -8.

ESCORT RATIO: 2 Builder Bots per forward turret, parked on 2 of its 4 orthogonal neighbours. That is the whole answer. Cost is 60 Ti of bodies once plus at most 2 Ti/round while actually under attack (0 Ti/round when undamaged, because can_heal is False at full HP). The enemy can then field at most 2 grinders for -4 HP/round against our +8 HP/round, and pays 4 Ti/round to our 2. A third escort adds nothing — measured (3,x) cells behave identically to (2,x).

Three concrete consequences:

1. Park the escort AT BUILD TIME, not on demand. In cells where healers walked in late they LOST the race for tiles: hg24x25 (N=3,M=3) reports CONTACT f=SW e=EN, so a grinder took the north tile and one of our three healers was locked out of its own turret. Whoever stands on the tile first owns it. The builder that constructs the turret should simply never leave.

2. Do not buy ammo to defend the turret from grinders. A Sentinel covers only 1 of its 4 contact tiles (facing line, ATK mask = EAST only) and spends 10 Ti/shot, ~30 Ti per grinder killed, versus 1 Ti/round for a healer that covers the tile permanently. Reserve ammo for the Core-killing job it is for.

3. Grinding an escorted building is a 4:1 losing exchange, which makes "send builders to chew their turret" a trap we should walk the OPPONENT into and never fall into ourselves. Send grinders only against buildings we can see are unescorted. Conversely, a forward turret that survives is a titanium pump: every 2 Ti they spend attacking it costs us 0.5 Ti to undo.

Extrapolation to be tested, not assumed: a Core is 2x2, so it has 8 orthogonal contact tiles and the arithmetic becomes 6k - 16, i.e. 3 healers minimum to hold a Core against a full grind ring. Do not reuse the "2 escorts" number for Core defence.
claimed.caveats:
1. THE BIGGEST HOLE: Launchers are untested here and are the obvious counter to a parked escort. A Launcher (20 Ti, r^2=26) picks up EITHER team's Builder Bot, so one enemy Launcher may be able to throw our garrison off its contact tiles and re-open the ring for free. Everything above assumes the escort cannot be displaced. This should be the very next probe — if a Launcher can evict a garrison, the escort ratio has to be re-derived.

2. No ore on the lab arenas, so both economies are pure passive Core income (10 Ti / 4 rounds, verified). The absolute bankruptcy rounds (attacker broke at ~r351) scale with harvester income and are not transferable; the PER-HIT and PER-HEAL costs (2 Ti / 1 Ti) and the 4:1 exchange ratio are structural and are.

3. Turret facing was fixed EAST in all runs; Gunner rotation (10 Ti) was never exercised. The ATK mask result — turret self-defence reaches exactly 1 of 4 contact tiles — is therefore a statement about a fixed facing, not about a rotating Gunner.

4. The (2,2) trace shows an unmodelled quirk of intra-round ordering: one healer engaged at r27 and the other only at the forced round 60, because units run in a fixed order within a round and only the healer running AFTER the grinders ever observed the dipped HP. The physics is unaffected (the +4/round segment with both healing is direct evidence of stacking), but a real bot must not gate healing on a threshold read at an arbitrary point in the turn order — just heal whenever can_heal is True, which costs nothing at full HP.

5. Every cell is n=1. That is the complete sample because the engine is deterministic (already established in commit 8cb0867 and re-confirmed here: five cells re-run after source edits produced byte-identical traces).

6. No CPU-time claims are made — get_cpu_time_elapsed() returns 0 on this machine.

7. The collar-mode reports label themselves "CFG GUN ... ammo=1" in the first width-28 run; that was a cosmetic bug in the label derivation, fixed before the final width-28 runs quoted above. ATK=5/1 and SHOTS=0 confirm those runs were an unfired Sentinel throughout.

verified.question: Can N friendly Builder Bots out-heal M enemy Builder Bots grinding a forward turret, and is a forward turret therefore holdable? (Task 1.1, fcode 2.3.6)

verified.design_impact:
Keep the arithmetic, throw away the word "mathematically". The escort works, but it is a footrace, not a theorem, and the bot has to be built around the race rather than around the ratio.

1. Measure TILES HELD, not escorts sent. The threshold is k >= 2 contact tiles, and "2 parked Builder Bots" equals "2 tiles" only if both bots actually arrive first. Every extra escort beyond the tiles you can occupy is 30 Ti of pure waste (hg28x21 proves it: 3 escorts, identical death round to 2).

2. Site the turret by ARRIVAL TIME, not by aggression. Build only where your escorts reach the contact tiles before the enemy's grinders. Escorts must leave with the constructor, not follow it. On the lab geometry the flip happened between Tx=12 (escort parks r10, holds) and Tx=17 (escort parks r15, enemy parked r11, dead r32).

3. There is no relief operation. Builder Bots cannot attack units, so once the enemy has parked on 3 tiles you cannot evict them with builders at any cost -- your relief force stands adjacent and does nothing. Eviction needs a Launcher (r^2=26, picks up either team's builder) or a turret with ammo, and the ammo route is measured-ruinous at 660 Ti for 66 Sentinel shots. Prefer conceding the turret to feeding it.

4. Turn the geometry around and use it defensively. The whole result is driven by contact-tile count, so a turret sited in a wall pocket with only 2 orthogonal neighbours needs just 1 escort to be unkillable by grinding, and one with 1 neighbour needs none. Siting for low contact-tile count is strictly better than siting forward and paying for escorts. (Geometric consequence of the verified orthogonal-only action rule; I did not build a walled arena to measure it.)

5. Do not carry this to the Core. A 2x2 Core has 8 orthogonal contact tiles, so the 2-escort rule does not transfer -- 2 escorts cover a quarter of it, and the break-even there is k >= 6 of 8.
verified.caveats:
What I could NOT break, and where my own test is soft:

- Nothing in the mechanical claims is stale or fabricated. HEAL_AMOUNT, BUILDER_BOT_HEAL_COST, BUILDER_BOT_ATTACK_DAMAGE and BUILDER_BOT_ATTACK_COST come straight out of 2.3.6 GameConstants, the orthogonal-only action range comes from docs/official/docs/game-rules-builder-bot.txt, and all 11 re-run cells matched. No zeros-from-__pycache__, no missing spawns (unit counts reconcile), no pre-2.3.4 numbers.

- My enemy is hand-routed, and that cuts both ways. With both sides on the naive greedy policy the three grinders bunch on the nearest tile and only ever claim 2, which flatters the original claim; giving them private lanes is what exposes the loss. A real rival will be somewhere between. The honest statement is that the outcome is decided by arrival order and both orderings are reachable, NOT that the enemy always wins.

- The forwardness threshold (between Tx=12 and Tx=17 on this arena) is specific to hg geometry: all-EMPTY terrain, spawn rings at x=3 and x=W-4. On a real map walls change travel distance and can also remove contact tiles. I did not build a walled arena.

- Untested counters I did not have time to measure: Launcher eviction of a parked escort, and an enemy barrier dropped on a contact tile before the escort arrives (3 Ti to deny a tile, which would make the race even harder to win). Both should be probed before anything ships.

- No tournament sweeps were run and no timing claims are made (Windows get_cpu_time_elapsed() returns 0).

- Scope note: "unkillable by grinding" is correctly scoped in the original -- a parked escort genuinely cannot be removed by another Builder Bot. The failure is upstream of that, in getting the escort parked at all.

claimed.headline: Build order decides the Sentinel duel completely — the turret with the lower global entity id fires first and survives at exactly 4/40 HP in 11/11 configurations — but a head start beyond winning the tie is worth 0 HP for a Sentinel and exactly +7 HP (one free shot) for a Gunner, because entity ids are a strictly ascending never-recycled counter and there is nothing to shoot at until the enemy turret exists.

claimed.design_impact: 1. "BUILD FIRST" IS A WIN CONDITION, but only because build order and entity id are the same thing. Ids are a strictly ascending global counter, never recycled, shared across both teams; the turret that exists first holds the lower id and therefore fires first for the rest of the match. There is no way to be late and still shoot first. 2. THE HP PAYOFF IS CAPPED AT ONE FREE SHOT and it is taken on the round the enemy turret is created (a fresh entity is shootable that round but does not act until the next). Gunner: 1 round of head start = +7 HP (survivor 11/25 instead of 4/25); rounds 2-8 add nothing. Sentinel: +0 HP at any head start — the survivor ends at 4/40 in all 11 configurations, because 3 shots kill and the loser lands 2 either way. So in a pure turret-vs-turret standoff, do NOT trade siting quality for arrival rounds beyond winning the tie: round 1 of head start is worth everything (it flips the duel), rounds 2 through 8 are worth zero. 3. WHERE EXTRA HEAD START PAYS IS DENIAL, AND ONLY FOR THE SENTINEL. Six rounds of Sentinel head start with fire on the tile the enemy builder must occupy kills that builder in its build slot and the enemy turret is never built at all (5/5 games at h>=6). The threshold is exactly 3 shots at cooldown 2 landing before the enemy's build round. A Gunner cannot do this at any head start: its 3-tile line stops one tile short of the builder's standing tile at a range-3 standoff. Turret siting should therefore optimise for a Sentinel whose 5-tile line covers the tiles an enemy builder must stand on, not merely the enemy turret tile. 4. NEVER CALL fire() ON A SENTINEL WITHOUT CHECKING THE TILE HOLDS AN ENEMY. can_fire() returns True on empty ground for a Sentinel (5/5 empty tiles) and fire() succeeds, burning 10 ammo; a Gunner correctly returns False. Worse than the ammo, the void shot puts the Sentinel on cooldown so it misses the free opening shot when the enemy turret finally appears — measured as the kill slipping from round 24 to round 25. Gate on get_tile_building_id()/get_tile_builder_bot_id() being non-None and enemy-owned, then can_fire(). 5. NO MUTUAL DESTRUCTION EXISTS. Resolution is strictly sequential, so any "we both die" contingency in combat logic is dead code — the lower-id unit always survives the exchange. 6. MIRRORED SCORING IS MANDATORY. On a symmetric map with symmetric openings, team A's Core is id 1, so its builder and then its turret both hold the lower id and team A wins every mirror duel. 7. OPENING TEMPO IS THE CHEAPEST LEVER IN THE GAME: one round earlier on the Core's first spawn propagates to every derived unit's id for the whole match.

verified.design_impact: Keep the mechanism, throw away the fatalism. (1) Turn order really is ascending global entity id, ids never recycle, and a turret created in round r cannot act until r+1 — so "build the Sentinel one round earlier, or place it from your lowest-id builder" is a genuine free win in an unsupported standoff, and "built later but with a lower id" is unconstructible. Use it. (2) But do NOT code the duel as pre-decided. Losing the id race is recoverable for 4 Ti: park one builder orthogonally adjacent to the Sentinel (on an off-axis tile, never in the enemy's cardinal lane) and heal every round. That flips the winner in both mirror directions. The defensive corollary is stronger than the offensive one — winning the id race is worth nothing if the enemy heals and you do not, so a Sentinel forward of your builders is a Sentinel you will lose. Pair every contested turret with a healer, and treat an unpaired enemy turret as the one you can actually kill. (3) The real prize for a big head start is not HP, it is denial: a free-firing Sentinel built 6+ rounds early kills the enemy builder standing in its build slot and the turret is never built at all (4/4). A Gunner cannot do this at any head start — 3-tile line vs 5. If you are racing for map control, race with Sentinels. (4) Gate Sentinel fire on an occupied tile unless you are deliberately denying: a Sentinel fires at empty ground at 10 ammo/shot and the wasted cooldown cost the opening shot in the claimed du_s_v4 comparison. (5) Never expect a mutual kill to save you — 0 in 24 decided duels; damage resolves strictly sequentially by id.
verified.caveats: Scope of the refutation: I reproduced EVERY number in the original claim, most of them byte-identical over 3 repeats. The engine mechanism (id-ordered turns, non-recycled ids, r+1 first action, no simultaneous kill) is solid and I found no counterexample. What fails is the universality of the headline: "decides the Sentinel duel COMPLETELY" and "there is nothing to shoot at until the enemy turret exists". Both are lab-arena conclusions from a probe whose turrets were forbidden to target anything but the enemy turret tile and whose builders deliberately walked out of the fight. Add the single cheapest realistic support unit and the conclusion inverts. The original claim's own free-fire numbers already contradicted its own causal clause; that contradiction was reported in the body but not carried into the headline. Other caveats: (a) everything is one 16x9 fully-open lab arena with turrets exactly 3 apart on a shared row — the mechanism generalises, the constants 4/40, 11/25, 10/40, 2/40 do not; on a real map a pure unsupported 1v1 Sentinel standoff is the rare case, not the default. (b) The claim reports the mirror configs (s_m1/m3/m4) killing on round 25; I measure round 24 (lastfire=24, dFOE observed 25 with the store's one-round lag). Minor, does not affect the headline. (c) I cannot separate "ordered by entity id" from "ordered by creation order" — they coincide by construction and ids never recycle, so no in-engine experiment can distinguish them. The claim says this correctly. (d) My first heal probe silently did nothing because I called a nonexistent ct.get_location(); the outer try/except swallowed the AttributeError and the run looked like a clean negative result identical to the control. I caught it only by checking the API surface. Flagging it because it is the same silent-zero failure class HARNESS.md warns about, and a probe that "confirms" a claim by no-oping is indistinguishable from one that measures it. (e) No timing or CPU claims are made — Windows cannot measure CPU. (f) I ran no tournament sweeps.

verified.design_impact: Four rules the bot must encode, and two API calls it must stop trusting. (1) The allied Core footprint is a WALL in path search — 64/64 measurements, all four tiles, all four approach directions, 8 maps. A builder cannot cut through its own base, so corridor and spawn-pocket logic must route around it, and the fcode docstring that says otherwise must not be believed. (2) Conveyors and Splitters do NOT block, for either team. A denial ring or a corridor plug must be built from Barrier (3 Ti), Harvester, or a turret; belts are worth zero denial. The mirror of that is offensive: enemy belts are a free highway, so attack pathing should treat enemy conveyor/splitter tiles as walkable rather than as obstacles. (3) can_move is NOT a passability oracle — it returns False on a verifiably passable tile whenever move_cd > 0. Use is_tile_passable to build the map model and can_move only for "may I act this instant"; conflating them makes the pathfinder hallucinate walls every other round. (4) is_tile_empty is not a step test: it is True under both own and enemy builder bots, so any code using it to pick a destination will walk into an occupied tile and eat a GameError. Two further constraints: is_tile_passable(own tile) is False, so a BFS that validates its own start node rejects every path; and is_tile_passable is vision-gated (raises beyond d_sq 20 for a builder, and checks vision BEFORE bounds), so a global map model must cache observations rather than query on demand. Finally, Harvesters block movement — auto-build must not harvest a corridor shut against its own builders.

claimed.design_impact:
Write the bot against 10 000 µs of CPU per unit per round, and stop treating 2 ms as a constraint — the 2e3 in the visualiser never fires on a real replay.

Concretely, four things change:

1. There is a large amount of unused headroom. bot/main.py peaks at 1289 µs on the two maps measured and sits at p50 = 12-30 µs, so we are using about 13% of the budget at worst and roughly 0.3% typically. Per-unit search, flood fills, and multi-step planning that were being avoided on a 2 ms assumption are affordable. At the measured Windows rates, 10 ms buys about 670 get_nearby_tiles() calls or 926 get_nearby_entities() calls per unit per round.

2. The budget is PER UNIT, so it scales with army size — 6 units burned 48 ms of team CPU in one round with nothing flagged. A 50-unit team has 500 ms of round budget. Do not build a team-wide compute governor; per-unit cost is what matters.

3. Precompute belongs in the module body, which is completely outside the per-turn clock (40 ms there cost round 0 exactly 49 µs). Distance tables, symmetry candidates, and map-derived constants should be computed at module scope, not lazily on round 0. Note each unit re-executes the module, so this trades wall-clock startup for turn-time safety.

4. The failure mode is a silent hard stop, not an exception and not a death. Everything the unit had already committed is kept; everything after the cut simply never happens, including prints, and try/except cannot see it. So order the round: issue the cheap high-value action FIRST, then do the expensive thinking. A unit that computes then acts loses its action entirely when it overruns; a unit that acts then computes loses only the refinement. luc1 loses 13 unit-turns this way on aurora.

Also correct HARNESS.md: print() is not swallowed. It is recorded in the replay as BotOutput.stdout, per unit per round, on Windows too (cpukeep: 13/13 rounds captured). It is only absent from run_game's result dict. That is a full-bandwidth per-unit debug channel that probes have not been using — but a print after the CPU cut is lost with the rest of the turn.

verified.design_impact: The 10 ms number stands, so nothing that was sized against 10 ms needs resizing — but the enforcement model in the verified note is wrong and that changes how the bot must be written. (1) The engine does NOT pre-empt Python. It stops the unit at its next Controller call after the budget is gone, silently, with no catchable exception. A heavy pure-Python planning phase will run to completion no matter how long it takes; the bot then dies at its next ct.* call and every action it had not yet issued that turn simply never happens (vcut2: zero ammo over 11 rounds where the tle=0 control got 11). (2) Therefore ordering is a hard rule: issue the highest-value action FIRST, then plan. Work committed before the overrun survives (ammo rose on 31/31 tled rounds). A bot that plans first and acts last loses the entire turn on an overrun; a bot that acts first loses only the tail. (3) Self-policing with ct.get_cpu_time_elapsed() still works and is the right tool, but be aware that call is itself a place the axe can fall — check early with margin and bail voluntarily. (4) Budget for ~10.0 ms, not 10.5: the +5% bank is real but only ~500 us and only on a turn that follows cheaper turns; consecutive heavy turns get 10 006-10 029 us. (5) Module-scope precompute is free (40 ms cost round 0 nothing), so push table building, map preprocessing and constant setup to import time. (6) The budget is per unit, so a 50-unit team gets ~500 ms/round — per-unit cost is the only thing that matters. (7) Ignore the visualiser's TLE overlay as a 2 ms signal; it renders the engine's tled flag and its 2e3 branch is unreachable. (8) All local Windows runs are timing-blind (every one of the 148 repo replays has execTimeUs=0), so any TLE gate in the harness must run under WSL with --tle, and must keep the repo's existing local-vs-ladder margin since the ladder is ARM.
verified.caveats: The verdict on the QUESTION (10 ms, not 2 ms) holds and is now re-derived by a second, independent method — counting units of work completed rather than reading execTimeUs. But one clause of the verified headline is refuted: "the engine hard-cuts a unit's turn at execTimeUs 10002-10009" is an artifact of the original probes, whose burn loops called ct.get_cpu_time_elapsed() every ~100 iterations. That polling is exactly what triggers the cut, which is why the overshoot looked like <=9 us. Remove the API calls and the same engine at the same tle=10 lets the turn run 110-138 ms. So execTimeUs is NOT bounded by the budget, and "tled" in a replay means "went over", not "was stopped at". Not re-verified by me, and I would not cite them without a re-run: the per-op microbenchmark table (get_nearby_tiles 14.9 us etc.) — those are Windows perf_counter numbers and the Linux/ARM constants will differ; and the real-bot percentiles for bot/main.py and luc1 (p50=30/p90=202, luc1 max=80 404 us) — bot/main.py is modified in the working tree, so those figures are not reproducible as stated. Finally, the ladder's own value of 10 is an inference from three documentation sources, not a measurement: the engine enforces precisely the turn_timeout_ms it is given, and no local probe can observe what the server passes.

claimed.design_impact:
THE DEFECT. bot/main.py stores `S_RUSHER = id + 1` once (line 1211) and never touches it again. When that builder dies the slot still names it, every other builder reads a non-zero claim and stands down permanently, and the attack never resumes. The obvious repair — ask whether the claimant is still alive — is impossible: st_id shows get_hp on a LIVE teammate raises GameError the moment it leaves the caller's vision (6 tiles for the Core), and a rusher at the enemy Core is never in vision of anything at home. Liveness must travel in the store.

THE PROTOCOL (drop-in, zero new slots).
Encoding, in the slot the id already occupies:
    word = (owner_id + 1) << 10 | (round the owner last renewed)
`word >> 10` is bit-for-bit the old `id + 1`, so the three existing read sites (bot/main.py lines 1209, 1221, 1596) need only `>> 10` added; `word == 0` still means unclaimed. Round < 1024 = MAX_TURNS 1000, so the stamp never wraps. Ids reach ~630 in a real game against the 4194302 ceiling.

Every unit, every round:
    raw   = read_store(S_RUSHER)
    stamp = raw & 1023
    held  = (raw >> 10) - 1
    fresh = raw != 0 and (round - stamp) < 2
    if raw and held == mine:   self.owner = True      # our claim came back — the role is ours
    elif fresh:                self.owner = False     # somebody live holds it
    if self.owner:
        write_store(S_RUSHER, ((mine + 1) << 10) | round)   # renew FIRST, unconditionally
        ...perform the role...
    elif not fresh:
        write_store(S_RUSHER, ((mine + 1) << 10) | round)   # challenge; resolves next round

Three measured facts make this correct with no handshake and no tie-break: (1) writes land exactly one round late, so the freshest stamp any reader can see is round-1 — STALE=2 is the tightest threshold that can never evict a living owner, and 1639 measured rounds produced 0 false evictions; (2) a same-round collision keeps the highest entity id, so when every idle builder challenges at once exactly one survives and the losers see a foreign id next round and stand down; (3) a write buffered in the round the owner dies still lands, so the lease is trustworthy right up to the last round the owner ran.

SLOT BUDGET — unchanged, all 16 still spoken for. 0 core x+1, 1 core y+1, 2 spawn ordinal, 3 state word (alarm bit0 + posture bits1-2), 4-8 ore claims, 9 S_RUSHER2 -> becomes a lease word, 10 enemy core anchor + SIGHTED, 11 symmetry mask + archetype evidence, 12 S_RUSHER -> becomes a lease word, 13 rush done latch, 14 rush ray, 15 rush active. Only slots 9 and 12 change meaning, and only in their low 10 bits.

CHOOSE THE VARIANT. Conservative (challenger waits one round to confirm): 2 vacant rounds, never more than one attacker on the board. Optimistic (challenger acts the round it challenges): 1 vacant round, but every idle builder performs the role for that one round — measured at 3 simultaneous actors. For the siege, take conservative: one wasted round is cheaper than three builders walking toward the enemy Core and then two of them turning around.

TWO CONSEQUENCES TO HANDLE. The cold-start claim also costs 2 rounds (challenge, then confirm), which is 1 round slower than today's write-then-confirm — the same handshake, so the rush start is unaffected. And the S_RUSH_DONE / S_RUSH_ACTIVE latches are role state, not unit state: they correctly survive the handover, so the successor inherits a finished route rather than rebuilding it, and no reset is needed.
claimed.caveats: Three limits on what was measured. (1) The kills were self_destruct, not enemy fire. Death by damage was never isolated — the owner survived all 5 rival games. The two measured modes bracket every possible cause though: either the owner's final turn included its renewal write (2 rounds vacant) or it did not (2 rounds vacant), and enemy fire must land in one of those. Both measure 2, so the result is cause-agnostic by construction, but it is an argument, not a third measurement. (2) The max-id figure is one observed number (627 at round 950 vs starter on sprint) plus a projection from a churn-maximising probe; a game with a much larger economy would mint more resource entities, though the 4500x headroom absorbs a lot. (3) Windows cannot measure CPU (get_cpu_time_elapsed returns 0), so the per-round cost of the extra write and mask is unmeasured here — it is one read, one write and two shifts, but that is asserted, not timed. Separately: resign_message is truncated at 500 characters, which cost one run and is worth adding to HARNESS.md.

verified.design_impact: Adopt the lease, but budget the vacancy as 2*(1+k), not 2. Concretely: (1) Replace the write-once claim at bot/main.py:1206-1228 with a renew-every-round lease word `(get_id()+1) << 10 | round` and change `if claim == mine:` to `if claim >> 10 == mine:` — it is not a drop-in read. (2) Renew UNCONDITIONALLY at the top of the owner's turn, before any code that can raise; the whole safety proof is "a live owner never misses a turn", and one exception thrown before the renew manufactures a false eviction that 22 games of engine behaviour will never show you. (3) Keep STALE=2. STALE=1 is not merely tight, it is degenerate — reads are a prior-round snapshot, so a stamp of `round` is unreachable and every unit permanently believes it owns the role. (4) For a role that must not stall under fire (a rush), do not use the optimistic variant to buy the 1-round vacancy: it makes every idle unit perform the role on the handover round (5 of 6 measured), which for a rush means the whole builder pool marching. Instead have the challenger publish the challenge and have the LOSERS re-challenge at `round - stamp >= 2` even against an unconfirmed claim, or accept 2*(1+k). (5) The 10-bit round field has only 23 rounds of headroom against MAX_TURNS=1000; if the round budget is ever raised the id field corrupts silently, so assert `round < 1024` at the pack site.
verified.caveats: Three things this verification cannot settle. (1) TLE: Windows returns 0 from get_cpu_time_elapsed() and the time limit is never enforced here, so a turn skipped because a unit blew its budget cannot be produced or ruled out on this machine. The "0 turn skips / 0 false evictions" numbers are measured only under no time pressure, and a TLE-skipped turn is precisely the event that would evict a living owner. (2) My builders do almost nothing per turn; a real bot's owner runs hundreds of lines before renewing, so the exception-before-renew risk is real and untested. (3) "Highest entity id wins the collision" is what is measured; the claim's gloss "i.e. units act in ascending id order and the last write of the round lands" remains an inference — the snapshot semantics I measured (A4) mean act order is not directly observable through the store at all. It does not affect the protocol, which only needs exactly one writer to survive. Separately, the 21-game contested sweep produced only 59 handovers, so a 1-in-59 event like the dead-claimant case is measured to roughly a factor of two; the mechanism is proven deterministically by vf_comp, but its FREQUENCY under fire is not.

claimed.design_impact:
STOP SHOOTING CONVEYORS AND LEAVING THE TILE EMPTY. That is the one thing the bot must not do. Measured: 2.18:1 against with a gunner, 6.69:1 against with a sentinel, and a denial window of exactly zero rounds because the victim replants inside the same round. The only titanium you take is the 25% of kills that happen to catch a stack — 2.5 Ti for your 12 Ti. Continuous sniping with one gunner eats 80% of a one-chain economy.

INSTEAD, TAKE AND HOLD THE TILE. Kill the terminal conveyor and put your own 3 Ti barrier on the vacated tile. destroy() is allied-only, so they must shoot it: 20 Ti minimum (5 gunner shots or 2 sentinel shots) plus turret capital plus a permanent +20% scale tax, against your 3 Ti. Uncontested this is 1:6.5 in your favour and denies 91% of their harvest.

FOUR IMPLEMENTATION CONSTRAINTS, ALL MEASURED:
1. Entity-id scheduling. The occupying builder must be spawned AFTER the turret that clears the tile, so it holds the higher id and acts later in the round. Get this backwards and it never once sees the tile empty — placed=0 over 800 rounds.
2. Use a SENTINEL for the clearing shot when your occupier stands in the lane. A gunner's line stops on your own builder; the sentinel's does not. On the only tile adjacent to their terminal conveyor, this is forced.
3. Heal the held building every round it is damaged: 1 Ti per 4 HP returns 2.7:1 against their ammo.
4. Target the TERMINAL conveyor tile — the one adjacent to their Core footprint. Cutting there zeroes the whole upstream chain (harvester and mid-conveyor untouched, collection still went to 180/1990).

BARRIER-ON-ORE is the best exchange in the game (1:622, 100% denial, blocks the harvester from ever being built) but it is only available on ore you reach FIRST. Home ore is unwinnable — you arrive round 14, their harvester has stood since round 3. Only contest midfield/equidistant ore, and only if you can commit a builder there in the opening.

ABANDON CONDITION — count how many times your own occupying building is destroyed, per 100 rounds. Uncontested measures 0.125; contested by an enemy turret measures 12.9. Cross 2 per 100 rounds and the exchange has collapsed from 1:6.5 to 1:1.33, and at 1:1.33 both economies are gone by round 800 (defender ended on 49 Ti, attacker on 987 vs a 4234 control). At that point stop paying for the clearing shots — hold the barrier only while it survives for free, and spend the sentinel's ammo somewhere that is not a 3 Ti conveyor.

SECOND ABANDON SIGNAL, cheaper to compute: if get_global_resources() is falling while your turret fires, you are converting your entire economy into their 3 Ti rebuilds. And remember the asymmetry that makes attrition unwinnable — their rebuild is a flat 3 Ti forever (destroyed buildings stop counting toward scale), while every turret you build is a permanent +20% on every price you pay.
claimed.caveats:
SCOPE — this is a mechanism measurement, not a ship-ready exploit. Per the standing constraint in HARNESS.md it has NOT been run against three rivals or on unseen maps. Everything here is one purpose-built arena (maps/lab/sab.map26, 22x10 open, ONE harvester chain and ONE ore per side) against two hand-written lab victims: sb_vic, the cheapest possible rebuilder, and sb_vics, the cheapest possible counter-battery. A real rival will sit somewhere between them.

DENIAL PERCENTAGES ARE UPPER BOUNDS. With one chain per side, cutting the terminal conveyor removes 100% of harvest income. A rival running three chains would see the same absolute Ti denied but a third of the percentage, and would need three occupations to reproduce these ratios — which triples the attacker's turret capital and its scale tax.

THE ORE FIGURE NEEDED A HANDICAP. The 1:622 barrier-on-ore number required delaying the victim 40 rounds (sb_vicd). Against a normal opening the race is lost outright (sb_ore vs sb_vic: placed=0, theirs=787). Treat 1:622 as the value of ore you already hold, never as a reason to send a builder at a defended ore tile.

TURN ORDER IS INFERRED, NOT READ. "Team A acts before team B, and within a team in entity-id order" is deduced from the placed=0 -> placed=103 flip between sb_occ and sb_occ2, not from engine source. It reproduces exactly, but it was only ever exercised with the saboteur as team A. If the bot sabotages as team B the ordering may not favour it, and the occupier-id trick needs re-measuring on that side.

CONTROLS ARE NOT PERFECT. sb_occ's attacker cost (3915 Ti) is compared against sb_warc, which builds a gunner rather than a sentinel and no third builder, so treat 6.69:1 as approximate; the belt-snipe (2.18:1) and occupy (1:6.5, 1:1.33) ratios all use matched controls and are exact. The defender's ammo spend in the contested-occupy case (317 sentinel shots) is back-computed from b_titanium rather than counted directly — team B has no reporting channel.

ALL RUNS ARE 800 ROUNDS OF A 1000-ROUND GAME, ended by the attacker resigning. Every figure reproduces bit-identically on re-run, consistent with the engine being deterministic. No timing or CPU claims are made — Windows returns 0 from get_cpu_time_elapsed().

The 2.3.3 note that a barrier on an ore tile denies 100% of that tile's output is re-confirmed on 2.3.6, as is destroy()/heal() being allied-only while fire() is team-blind, and that only stacks landing on a Core footprint tile count toward titanium_collected. One correction worth recording: titanium_collected counts ORE DELIVERED ONLY and excludes the 10 Ti/4 rounds passive, so it is a clean harvest meter (measured 2.49 Ti/round per chain).

verified.design_impact: Keep the belt-snipe prohibition — it is measured, robust, and applies to both gunner (2.18:1) and sentinel (6.70:1, zero denial). Do NOT ship the cut-then-occupy plan the finding recommends: its 1:6.5 evaporates against the cheapest generic defence, and the attacker cannot tell the difference from inside its own bot — the occupier's observable state (placed=1, ours=723/800, heals=0) is byte-identical in the game where it denied 91% and the game where it denied 1%. So the finding's proposed abandon condition ('occupying-building replacements per 100 rounds, threshold 2') is unsound: in the refutation run replacements were 0.125/100 rounds, comfortably under threshold, i.e. the bot would have held a worthless tile for 723 rounds and called it a win. Any occupation logic must gate on the victim's actual delivery rate, not on tile tenure, and must budget for holding up to 8 core-intake tiles rather than 1. Two genuinely portable takeaways survive: (1) heal +4 HP/1 Ti strictly beats builder attack 2 dmg/2 Ti, so a barrier with a builder beside it cannot be removed by builders at all — only turret fire clears it, which is worth knowing on both offence and defence; (2) our own economy should carry the sb_vicr reroute behaviour, since 4 conveyors reduced a 1852 Ti loss to 74 Ti.
verified.caveats: The 2.3.3 baseline of 6.3:1 cannot be reproduced on this machine — no 2.3.3 engine is installed — so only the 2.3.6 number is measured; the claim that the ratio 'changed' from 6.3:1 to 2.18:1 rests on a note, not a run. The finding's sentinel figure of '3915 Ti attacker' borrowed sb_warc (a gunner build) as the control for a sentinel run; the ammo spend measured directly (392 fires x 10 Ti = 3920 Ti) happens to agree, so the conclusion stands but the control was mismatched. All runs are single-seed; a prior commit in this repo records the engine as fully deterministic and my re-runs of sb_war/sb_occ2/sb_occ2c matched the original digits exactly, which supports that. My sb_vicr bypass is safe from this particular attacker rig by construction — a re-aiming attacker was not measured; what is measured is that the defender's counter costs 74 Ti while the attacker's committed rig (sentinel + two builders, 285 Ti of spend) is stranded, and that there are 8 intake tiles to chase. Barrier-on-ore's 1:622 remains real but reachable only against an opponent that idles ~40 rounds, which is not a real opening.
